13077: John: The Word Who Tabernacled Among Us
13078:
John's Gospel is the most Jewish and the most argued-over of the four Gospels. It opens with the first words of Genesis, it is built around Israel's festivals (Passover, Sukkot, Hanukkah, the Sabbath), and it presents Jesus as the place where Israel's God now dwells: the Word, the true temple, the living water, the light of the world, the good shepherd. At the same time it contains some of the New Testament's sharpest words against 'the Jews', words that were later used to harm Jewish people. A careful reading has to hold both facts together.

The book tells us its own purpose: it was written so that readers would keep trusting that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that by trusting they would have life in his name (John 20:31). 'Life' here is not only life after death. In John it is 'the life of the age to come' already tasted now, and it is defined relationally: knowing the one true God and Jesus whom he sent (John 17:3).

This study walks through all 21 chapters. For each one it gives the story, the historical background (who wrote, where, and what conflict lay behind it), the cultural keys (feasts, weddings, wells, shepherds, burial and crucifixion), a Jewish covenant reading, what the first hearers would have felt, what it means today, Old Testament echoes, and common misreadings. It also lays out the main scholarly views on authorship and on the book's relationship to Judaism, so you can weigh them yourself.
13079: Read John as a Jewish book about Israel's God keeping covenant with his people, written in a time of painful family conflict. Its first audience heard Genesis in its opening line, Moses and the tabernacle in its talk of glory, and the festivals of Jerusalem in its middle chapters. Its big claim is that the God who once spoke creation into being, led Israel through the wilderness and dwelt in the temple has now come in person, in a Jewish man, to make his people (and through them the world) his friends. 'Believing' in John means ongoing trust and loyalty, a relationship, not a single mental assent. And the book's harsh words about 'the Jews' belong to an argument inside the Jewish family, mostly aimed at Judean leaders, not to a verdict on the Jewish people.
13081: 'In the beginning' deliberately echoes Gen 1:1. God's Word (Hebrew dabar, Aramaic memra) and Wisdom were already ways Jews spoke of God acting in the world. John says that this Word is personal and has become flesh. A Jewish hearer would recognise the categories before being startled by the claim.
13083: 'The Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us' (John 1:14) recalls the tabernacle in the wilderness and the glory cloud that filled it. Throughout John, Jesus' body is the new meeting place of God and people (John 2:21), so the loss of the Jerusalem temple in AD 70 is answered, not ignored.
13085: Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for Passover, Sukkot (Tabernacles) and Hanukkah (Dedication), and heals on the Sabbath. At each feast he takes up its central symbols (bread, water, light, the consecrated temple, rest) and says they find their meaning in him. Jesus is not opposed to Israel's calendar; he keeps it, as a faithful Jew, and fills it.
13086: 'I AM' and the one God of Israel
13087: Jesus' 'I am' sayings echo how God names himself in Exod 3:14 and especially in Isaiah (Isa 43:10, Isa 43:25), where 'I am he' is the language of Israel's one God. John is not leaving Jewish monotheism behind; he is claiming Jesus belongs inside the identity of the one God of the Shema (Deut 6:4).
13088: Life of the age to come, known in relationship
13089: Zōē aiōnios is usually translated 'eternal life', but in Jewish idiom it is 'the life of the age to come' (Dan 12:2). John's surprise is that this future life starts now, and he defines it as knowing God (John 17:3). In Hebrew thought 'knowing' is covenant intimacy, not just information.
13091: John never uses the noun 'faith' (pistis); he uses the verb 'believe/trust' (pisteuō) about 98 times. It is something you keep doing. Characters move toward or away from Jesus over time (Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, the blind man, Thomas). Trust is a journey of relationship, often shown by 'remaining' (menō) with Jesus.
13093: Hoi Ioudaioi can mean Judeans (people of Judea, as opposed to Galileans), the Jewish people, or, very often in John, the religious authorities in Jerusalem who oppose Jesus. Jesus, his mother, all the disciples and the narrator's first community were Jews. The harsh language reflects a bitter family quarrel, not a charge against the Jewish people of any age.
13095: John's picture of salvation is relational: God's children born 'from above' (John 1:12-13), sheep who know the shepherd's voice (John 10:14), servants made friends (John 15:15), and a new family formed at the cross (John 19:26-27). This is covenant language from Ezekiel 34 and Jeremiah 31 made personal.
13096: Jewish followers of Jesus, some pushed out of synagogue life
13097: Grief and anger at losing their place among family and neighbours; wondering whether following Jesus meant losing the festivals, Torah and temple; needing assurance that Jesus is truly Israel's Messiah (John 9:22, John 16:2).
13098: Gentile believers in a city such as Ephesus
13099: Learning the Jewish story they had joined; hearing that they are the 'other sheep' brought into one flock (John 10:16); needing explanations of Hebrew terms, which John supplies (John 1:38, John 1:41).
13100: Secret sympathisers still in the synagogue
13101: Like Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea, people who believed but feared open loyalty (John 12:42); the Gospel invites them to step into the light (John 19:38-39).
13103: The Gospel repeatedly says the Baptist was not the light but a witness to it (John 1:8, John 3:30); some scholars think Baptist loyalists were part of the audience (compare Acts 19:1-7 at Ephesus).
13104: Believers drawn to a 'spiritual' Christ without real flesh
13105: Early docetic ideas (that Jesus only seemed to be human) may lie behind the stress on flesh, blood, water, tears and touchable wounds (John 1:14, John 19:34, John 20:27); 1 John 4:2 confronts this directly.
13107: The prologue retells Genesis 1: the Word who was with God and was God has come into the world, pitched his tent among Israel and shown the Father's glory, full of covenant love and faithfulness (John 1:14, compare Exod 34:6).
13109: John the Baptist points to the Lamb of God; disciples follow and receive Jewish titles for Jesus: Rabbi, Messiah, the one Moses wrote about, King of Israel, Son of Man.
13111: Seven signs reveal who Jesus is: water to wine (2), the official's son (4), the paralysed man (5), feeding the 5,000 (6), walking on water (6), the man born blind (9), the raising of Lazarus (11). Each provokes faith in some and resistance in others.
13112: New temple, new birth, true worship
13113: Jesus clears the temple and speaks of his body as the temple; he tells Nicodemus of birth from above and the Samaritan woman of worship in Spirit and truth. Old institutions are not mocked but fulfilled.
13115: Sabbath (5), Passover (6), Sukkot (7-9) and Hanukkah (10): at each festival Jesus claims its symbols — Sabbath work, manna, water, light, the consecrated one — and controversy with the Jerusalem authorities grows.
13116: Lazarus and the decision to kill
13117: The greatest sign, Lazarus raised, triggers the council's decision that one man should die for the nation. Jesus is anointed for burial, enters Jerusalem as king, and the hour arrives. The Book of Signs closes with Isaiah's words about unbelief.
13119: On the eve of Passover Jesus washes his disciples' feet, gives the new commandment of love, and predicts betrayal and denial. Glory in John is shown by humble self-giving.
13121: Like Jacob or Moses before death, Jesus gives a farewell speech: the Father's house, the Paraclete (Spirit), the vine and branches, coming persecution, and his prayer that the disciples be one and share God's love.
13122: Arrest, trial and the lifted-up king
13123: Jesus goes to death in control: 'I am' in the garden, a king before Pilate, crucified as the Passover lambs are slaughtered, saying 'It is finished', buried as a king with lavish spices.
13125: Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus in a garden; he breathes the Spirit on the disciples as God breathed into Adam; Thomas confesses 'My Lord and my God'.
13127: John 20:30-31 states the aim: these signs are written so that you may keep trusting that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and have life in his name.
13129: By the Sea of Galilee Jesus feeds the disciples, restores Peter with three questions of love and commissions him to shepherd; the Beloved Disciple's testimony is affirmed as true.
13130: The Word, the Lamb and the first disciples
13131: John opens 'in the beginning' with the Word who was with God and was God, through whom everything was made. The Word is life and light; the world did not recognise him and his own people largely did not receive him, but those who did became God's children. The Word became flesh and 'tabernacled' among us, full of grace and truth. Then the story begins: John the Baptist denies being the Messiah, Elijah or the Prophet, and points to Jesus as 'the Lamb of God'. Andrew, Peter, Philip and Nathanael follow, giving Jesus a cascade of titles: Rabbi, Messiah, the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Son of God, King of Israel. Jesus promises they will see angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man.
13132:
Who wrote this? The book itself only says its witness is 'the disciple whom Jesus loved' (John 21:20-24). Irenaeus, around AD 180, said this was John son of Zebedee, who published the Gospel at Ephesus in old age. Many modern scholars think the Gospel took shape in stages within a community gathered around this disciple, finished around AD 90. Richard Bauckham argues the Beloved Disciple was a Jerusalem disciple called John the Elder, whom the early writer Papias mentions alongside the apostles.

Ephesus was a large Greek city in Asia Minor (modern Turkey) with a substantial Jewish community, and Acts records that disciples of John the Baptist were there (Acts 19:1-7). That may explain why chapter 1 is so careful to say the Baptist was a witness, not the light (John 1:8). The Jerusalem temple had been destroyed by Rome in AD 70, so a Gospel that calls Jesus God's 'tabernacle' would speak to a grieving people.
13133:
'Word' (logos) worked in two worlds at once. For Greek listeners, Stoic philosophers spoke of the Logos as the reason ordering the universe. For Jewish listeners, God created by speaking (Gen 1:3), his word 'ran swiftly' (Ps 147:15), Wisdom was beside him at creation (Prov 8:30), and the Aramaic Targums (synagogue paraphrases of scripture) often spoke of God's Memra (Word) acting in creation and history. The Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria, a contemporary of Jesus, called the Logos God's 'firstborn' and even a 'second God'.

The Baptist's questioners are priests and Levites sent from Jerusalem (John 1:19) — the temple establishment checking a rival movement. 'Lamb of God' would evoke the Passover lamb, the daily temple lambs and the servant led like a lamb to slaughter (Isa 53:7). 'Come and see' and 'where are you staying?' reflect how disciples attached themselves to a rabbi: by living with him.
13134:
The prologue is best heard as a Jewish meditation on Genesis 1 and on the Exodus. Light shines in darkness as at creation; the Word 'tabernacles' as God's glory filled the tent in the wilderness (Exod 40:34-35); 'grace and truth' echoes God's self-description to Moses as 'abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness' (Exod 34:6). Moses could not see God's face (Exod 33:20), but the only Son 'who is at the Father's side' has made him known (John 1:18).

Daniel Boyarin, a Jewish scholar of the Talmud, argues that the idea of a divine Word alongside God was not foreign to first-century Jews; what made John distinctive was saying this Word became a particular human being. 'His own' who did not receive him (John 1:11) are first of all Israel, yet the receivers are also Israelites — Andrew, Peter, Nathanael, 'an Israelite in whom there is no deceit'. Jacob's ladder (Gen 28:12) is applied to Jesus: he is the new Bethel, the 'house of God', where heaven and earth meet.
13135: Jewish believers who had lost the temple and, perhaps, their synagogue would hear: God's presence has not left you; it has been among you in a person. Gentile hearers would hear that the reason behind the universe has a name and a face. Followers of the Baptist would hear their teacher himself saying 'he must increase'. And everyone would hear an invitation to the same simple step the first disciples took: 'come and see'.
13136: The prologue resists both a merely human Jesus and a ghostly, unreal one. God is known not first through ideas but through a life lived in flesh. And discipleship begins as it did for Andrew: by spending time with Jesus and then bringing a brother.
13137: 'In the beginning', light and darkness, creation by speech.
13138: Glory filling the tent: the Word 'tabernacled' among us.
13139: 'Steadfast love and faithfulness' behind 'grace and truth'.
13140: The voice in the wilderness preparing the Lord's way.
13141: Jacob's ladder: angels ascending and descending, now on the Son of Man.
13142: John's Logos is a borrowing from Greek philosophy, so the prologue is a 'Greek' introduction to an un-Jewish Gospel.
13143: The prologue is rooted in Genesis, Wisdom and Exodus; Greek hearers would catch resonance, but its world is Jewish (Brown, Keener, Boyarin).
13144: Wine at Cana, fire in the temple
13145: At a wedding in Cana of Galilee the wine runs out. Jesus' mother tells him; he says his hour has not yet come, but she tells the servants to do whatever he says. Jesus has six stone water jars, used for Jewish purification, filled to the brim — about 120 to 180 gallons — and the water becomes excellent wine. This is 'the first of his signs', revealing his glory, and his disciples trust him. Then at Passover in Jerusalem Jesus drives out the animal sellers and money changers from the temple courts. Asked for a sign, he says, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.' John explains he meant the temple of his body, which the disciples understood only after the resurrection.
13146: John places the temple action at the start of Jesus' ministry, while Matthew, Mark and Luke place it in the last week. Scholars debate whether there were two incidents or whether John moved it to the front for theological reasons, to frame the whole ministry with the replacement of the temple by Jesus' body. Writing after AD 70, John's readers knew the temple had in fact been destroyed. 'Forty-six years' to build this temple (John 2:20) fits Herod's rebuilding begun around 20/19 BC, pointing to about AD 27/28.
13147:
Jewish weddings in Galilee could last up to a week, and the groom's family hosted. Running out of wine was a serious public shame: hospitality and honour were bound up with providing for guests, and some scholars suggest gifts of wine created reciprocal obligations. Mary's 'they have no wine' is a request made on behalf of the family.

The six stone jars matter. Stone, unlike pottery, was believed not to contract ritual impurity, and stone vessels have been found widely in first-century Judea and Galilee, including near Cana. They held water for hand-washing and purification. Jesus does not pour the water out; he transforms it. In the temple, money changers exchanged coins into the Tyrian shekel required for the temple tax, and animals were sold for pilgrims who could not bring their own. The trade was legal and useful; Jesus' protest is about it filling the space of prayer and turning 'my Father's house' into a marketplace.
13148:
Abundant wine was a prophetic picture of the messianic age: 'the mountains shall drip sweet wine' (Amos 9:13), and the Lord would make a feast of 'well-aged wines' for all peoples (Isa 25:6). A wedding was itself an image of God and Israel (Isa 62:4-5). So the first sign announces that the long-promised feast has begun, using Israel's own purification jars as the containers of the new.

In the temple Jesus acts like a prophet. The disciples recall 'zeal for your house will consume me' (Ps 69:9), and Zechariah had foreseen a day when there would no longer be a trader in the house of the Lord (Zech 14:21). His word about raising the temple in three days makes his body the true meeting place of God and people. This is not contempt for the temple: Jesus calls it 'my Father's house'. It is the claim that what the temple pointed to is now present in him.
13149: For Jewish readers after AD 70, the question 'where do we meet God now?' was raw. John answers: in the risen body of Jesus. The wedding scene also reassured them that following Jesus was not a sad loss of Jewish life but joy overflowing from within it — the jars of purification filled with wine.
13150: Jesus' first sign is an act of kindness that spares a family shame at a party. The God of John is generous and joyful. The temple scene warns religious communities whenever worship becomes business, and points to Jesus himself as the centre of worship.
13151: Mountains dripping with wine in the restored age.
13152: God's feast of fine wines for all peoples.
13153: 'Zeal for your house will consume me.'
13154: No more traders in the house of the Lord on that day.
13155: 'Do whatever he tells you' — Pharaoh's words about Joseph, echoed by Mary.
13156: The temple cleansing shows Jesus rejecting Jewish religion and its sacrifices as dead ritual.
13157: Jesus defends 'my Father's house' like the prophets did; his body becomes the temple's fulfilment, not a condemnation of Israel's worship (Coloe, Keener).
13158: Nicodemus: birth from above and the lifted-up Son
13159: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and member of the ruling council, comes to Jesus at night and calls him a teacher from God. Jesus tells him no one can see God's kingdom without being born anōthen — 'again' or 'from above'. Nicodemus takes it literally; Jesus speaks of being born of water and Spirit, and of the Spirit as wind blowing where it wills. Jesus says the Son of Man must be lifted up as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so that whoever trusts may have eternal life — 'for God so loved the world'. Light has come, and people reveal themselves by coming to it or avoiding it. The chapter ends with John the Baptist rejoicing as 'the friend of the bridegroom': 'He must increase, but I must decrease.'
13160: Nicodemus is one of John's most carefully drawn characters. He appears three times: coming by night (John 3:2), cautiously defending Jesus in the council (John 7:50-51), and finally bringing about 75 pounds of spices for Jesus' burial (John 19:39). Many scholars think he represented a group in John's own day: synagogue members who were sympathetic to Jesus but afraid to say so openly (John 12:42). The dialogue slides from Jesus' voice into the narrator's reflection, and translations disagree where the quotation marks end (after 3:15 or 3:21).
13161: Visiting a teacher at night was not necessarily cowardly; rabbis were known to study Torah at night. But in John, night and darkness carry symbolic weight (John 13:30). 'The teacher of Israel' marks Nicodemus as a recognised scholar. The 'friend of the bridegroom' (John 3:29) was the groom's best man, who arranged the wedding and rejoiced at the groom's joy, not seeking the bride for himself.
13162:
Jesus expects 'the teacher of Israel' to understand (John 3:10), which points us to Israel's scriptures. Ezekiel promised that God would sprinkle clean water on his people and put a new spirit within them (Ezek 36:25-27), and in the valley of dry bones the 'wind/breath/spirit' (ruach) would bring dead Israel to life (Ezek 37:9-14). 'Born of water and Spirit' is that promised renewal.

Then Jesus turns to Numbers 21. When the people were dying from snake bites, God told Moses to set a bronze serpent on a pole; whoever looked at it lived. Jewish tradition (for example the Wisdom of Solomon 16:6-7 and the Mishnah, Rosh Hashanah 3:8) stressed that it was not the bronze that healed but turning the heart to God. 'Lifted up' (hypsoō) in John means both crucified and exalted (John 12:32-33). John 3:16 explains the logic: God loved the world 'in this way' — by giving his Son to be lifted up so the dying could look and live.
13163: Secret believers would recognise themselves in Nicodemus and be gently urged toward the light. All hearers would be reminded that new life is God's gift, as surprising as the wind, and that it arrives through the cross, just as healing came to Israel in the wilderness through what God provided.
13164: The famous verse lives inside a story of a cautious, honest seeker who takes years to step into the open. God's love is costly and wide, embracing 'the world', and new birth is something God does, not a technique we perform.
13165: The bronze serpent: look and live.
13166: Clean water and a new spirit for Israel.
13167: Wind/Spirit giving life to dry bones.
13169: 'Your only son, whom you love' — the giving of a beloved son.
13170: John 3:16 stands alone as a summary: believe and you go to heaven when you die; 'born again' means praying a decision prayer.
13171: 3:16 completes 3:14-15 (the lifted-up serpent); 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, starting now; new birth 'from above' is the Spirit's renewal promised in Ezekiel (Keener, Thompson, Carson).
13173: Travelling through Samaria, a tired Jesus sits by Jacob's well at noon and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink — breaking norms of gender, ethnicity and purity. He offers 'living water' that becomes a spring welling up to eternal life. He shows he knows her history of five husbands, and she raises the old dispute: should God be worshipped on this mountain (Gerizim) or in Jerusalem? Jesus says salvation is from the Jews, yet the hour is coming when true worshippers will worship the Father in Spirit and truth. She says the Messiah is coming; Jesus answers, 'I am he, the one speaking to you.' She leaves her water jar and brings her town, and many Samaritans believe, calling him 'Saviour of the world'. Back in Cana, Jesus heals a royal official's son with a word: the second sign.
13174: Jews and Samaritans shared descent from Israel and the five books of Moses, but had been divided for centuries. Samaritans worshipped on Mount Gerizim; the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed their temple there in the late second century BC (Josephus places it around 128 BC; excavations suggest about 111-110 BC), and bitterness ran deep. The narrator explains 'Jews do not share things in common with Samaritans' (John 4:9), suggesting some readers needed this explained. Acts 8 shows Samaritans responding to the gospel early, and some scholars think Samaritan believers were part of John's community.
13175:
Wells were meeting places, and in Israel's stories they are where future marriages begin: Abraham's servant meets Rebekah (Gen 24), Jacob meets Rachel (Gen 29), Moses meets Zipporah (Exod 2:15-21). A first audience would sense a 'betrothal scene' — but here it becomes a bond between Jesus and a whole people. 'Living water' meant running water from a spring, as opposed to still cistern water; it was the purest kind for purification.

Why noon? Some say she was avoiding other women out of shame; others note noon is simply when a traveller would rest, and that the text never calls her immoral. Five husbands may reflect widowhood, divorce by men (women could rarely initiate divorce) or levirate marriage; the current man may be a relative supporting her. Jesus' word reveals knowledge, not condemnation, and she becomes the first evangelist to a town.
